# Title:Synaptic Dendritic Neuron Model (scDNM) for Cell Type Classification in Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Data
> Abstract:Cell type classification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is challenging because of high dimensionality, sparsity, and transcriptionally similar cell types. We developed scDNM, an adaptation of the dendritic neuron model incorporating learnable synaptic thresholds, a supervised gene pool, staged training, and ensemble prediction. Six binary classification tasks were constructed from the Paul15, PBMC3k, and Nestorowa datasets.
All models were evaluated using leakage-free nested cross-validation, with feature selection, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning performed independently of the outer test folds. scDNM ranked first in three of six tasks (including one tie) and achieved the best mean accuracy rank (2.00), followed by XGBoost (2.75), Random Forest (3.33), logistic regression (3.33), and SVM (3.58).
In a six-class PBMC3k experiment, scDNM achieved 95.997% accuracy and 0.944 macro-F1, compared with 94.243% and 0.914 for SingleR.  Ablation analysis supported the contributions of dendrites and synaptic thresholds.
However, XGBoost achieved higher mean binary-task accuracy (96.20% versus 95.32% for scDNM), and across-task rank differences were not statistically significant. These findings demonstrate that scDNM is competitive for scRNA-seq cell type classification, although broader independent validation is required.

# scDNM-VAE: Interpretable deep clustering of single-cell RNA-seq data with signed dendritic gating
###### Abstract
Deep clustering models for single-cell RNA sequencing commonly assign cells through latent distances or centroid-based rules that are difficult to inspect directly. We introduce scDNM-VAE (single-cell Dendritic Neuron Model Variational Autoencoder), which couples a variational encoder to a signed dendritic clustering head.
## 2 Results
### 2.1 Model architecture
Figure 1: The dendritic neuron model and the scDNM-VAE Stage-1 clustering head. (a) Computation flow of the classical DNM [2, 3]. Each input x_i reaches each branch j through its own synapse, gated by y_(ij)=σ(k(w_(ij)x_i-q_(ij))), where k>0 sets the gating sharpness.
Figure 2: scDNM-VAE training and interpretation workflow. (a) Stage 1 learns a 10-dimensional variational representation and cluster assignments through signed weight–threshold gates. Posterior means from pretraining initialize KMeans centres, which initialize W_(syn) and Q_(syn) and define the unsupervised occupancy prior.
## 3 Discussion
In this study, we proposed scDNM-VAE, a two-stage model for deep clustering of single-cell RNA-sequencing data that computes cluster membership using learned signed weights and thresholds. Comparisons across four benchmark datasets with distinct biological structures showed that scDNM-VAE provided a directly inspectable decision function while ranking among the two best-performing methods on every dataset.
The cluster-assignment mechanism of scDNM-VAE, which consists of signed weights and thresholds, allows researchers to directly examine the direction and transition points of latent dimensions involved in assigning a cell to a particular cluster. This property may make the method a useful alternative in single-cell studies where auditing cluster decisions and translating them into biological hypotheses are important.

# Title:Synaptic Dendritic Neuron Model (scDNM) for Cell Type Classification in Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Data
> Abstract:Cell type classification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is challenging because of high dimensionality, sparsity, and transcriptionally similar cell types. We developed scDNM, an adaptation of the dendritic neuron model incorporating learnable synaptic thresholds, a supervised gene pool, staged training, and ensemble prediction. Six binary classification tasks were constructed from the Paul15, PBMC3k, and Nestorowa datasets.

All models were evaluated using leakage-free nested cross-validation, with feature selection, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning performed independently of the outer test folds. scDNM ranked first in three of six tasks (including one tie) and achieved the best mean accuracy rank (2.00), followed by XGBoost (2.75), Random Forest (3.33), logistic regression (3.33), and SVM (3.58).

In a six-class PBMC3k experiment, scDNM achieved 95.997% accuracy and 0.944 macro-F1, compared with 94.243% and 0.914 for SingleR.

However, XGBoost achieved higher mean binary-task accuracy (96.20% versus 95.32% for scDNM), and across-task rank differences were not statistically significant. These findings demonstrate that scDNM is competitive for scRNA-seq cell type classification, although broader independent validation is required.

**Decision Trees (DTs)** are a non-parametric supervised learning method used for [classification](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html#tree-classification) and [regression](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html#tree-regression). The goal is to create a model that predicts the value of a target variable by learning simple decision rules inferred from the data features. A tree can be seen as a piecewise constant approximation.

For instance, in the example below, decision trees learn from data to approximate a sine curve with a set of if-then-else decision rules. The deeper the tree, the more complex the decision rules and the fitter the model.

[![Image 1: ../_images/sphx_glr_plot_tree_regression_001.png](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/_images/sphx_glr_plot_tree_regression_001.png)](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/tree/plot_tree_regression.html)

*   The cost of using the tree (i.e., predicting data) is logarithmic in the number of data points used to train the tree.

*   Able to handle both numerical and categorical data. However, the scikit-learn implementation does not support categorical variables for now. We developed scDNM, an adaptation of the dendritic neuron model incorporating learnable synaptic thresholds, a supervised gene pool, staged training, and ensemble prediction. Six binary classification tasks were constructed from the Paul15, PBMC3k, and Nestorowa datasets. All models were evaluated using leakage-free nested cross-validation, with feature selection, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning performed independently of the outer test folds. scDNM ranked first in three of six tasks (including one tie) and achieved the best mean accuracy rank (2.00), followed by XGBoost (2.75), Random Forest (3.33), logistic regression (3.33), and SVM (3.58). In a six-class PBMC3k experiment, scDNM achieved 95.997% accuracy and 0.944 macro-F1, compared with 94.243% and 0.914 for SingleR. keenable.snippet: We introduce scDNM-VAE (single-cell Dendritic Neuron Model Variational Autoencoder), a deep clustering framework that combines a variational autoencoder with a dendritic neuron-inspired head. ## Abstract  
Cell type classification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is challenging because of high dimensionality, sparsity, and transcriptionally similar cell types. We developed scDNM, an adaptation of the dendritic neuron model incorporating learnable synaptic thresholds, a supervised gene pool, staged training, and ensemble prediction. However, XGBoost achieved higher mean binary-task accuracy (96.20% versus 95.32% for scDNM), and across-task rank differences were not statistically significant. These findings demonstrate that scDNM is competitive for scRNA-seq cell type classification, although broader independent validation is required.

octen.title: Density-based Clustering with Best-scored Random Forest
octen.snippet:
Single-level density-based approach has long been widely acknowledged to be a
conceptually and mathematically convincing clustering method. In this paper, we
propose an algorithm called "best-scored clustering forest" that can obtain the
optimal level and determine corresponding clusters. The terminology
"best-scored" means to select one random tree with the best empirical
performance out of a certain number of purely random tree candidates. From the
theoretical perspective, we first show that consistency of our proposed
algorithm can be guaranteed. Moreover, under certain mild restrictions on the
underlying density functions and target clusters, even fast convergence rates
can be achieved. Last but not least, comparisons with other state-of-the-art
clustering methods in the numerical experiments demonstrate accuracy of our
algorithm on both synthetic data and several benchmark real data sets. stat.ML, cs.LG H. Hang, Yuchao Cai, Hanfang Yang

octen.title: Tree-based methods for estimating heterogeneous model performance and model combining
octen.snippet: Model performance is frequently reported only for the overall population under consideration. However, due to heterogeneity, overall performance measures often do not accurately represent model performance within specific subgroups. We develop tree-based methods for the data-driven identification of subgroups with differential model performance, where splitting decisions are made to maximize heterogeneity in performance between subgroups. We extend these methods to tree ensembles, including both random forests and gradient boosting. Lastly, we illustrate how these ensembles can be used for model combination. We evaluate the methods through simulations and apply them to lung cancer screening data. stat.ME Ruotao Zhang, C. Gatsonis, Jon Steingrimsson

octen.snippet:
There is a keen interest in characterizing variation in the microbiome across
cancer patients, given increasing evidence of its important role in determining
treatment outcomes. Here our goal is to discover subgroups of patients with
similar microbiome profiles. We propose a novel unsupervised clustering
approach in the Bayesian framework that innovates over existing model-based
clustering approaches, such as the Dirichlet multinomial mixture model, in
three key respects: we incorporate feature selection, learn the appropriate
number of clusters from the data, and integrate information on the tree
structure relating the observed features. We compare the performance of our
proposed method to existing methods on simulated data designed to mimic real
microbiome data. We then illustrate results obtained for our motivating data
set, a clinical study aimed at characterizing the tumor microbiome of
pancreatic cancer patients. stat.AP Yu-Shu Shi, Liangliang Zhang, K. Do, R. Jenq, Christine B. Peterson

Authors: J.E. Gonzales, S. Sim\'on-D\'iaz, S. Cuellar, J.A. Conejero, G. Holgado, A. de Burgos
Submitted: 2026-09-16
Subjects: astro-ph.SR

Journal reference: A&A 715, A234 (2026)
DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202662236

Abstract

[Abridged] The advent of large-scale spectroscopic surveys will deliver tens of thousands of spectra of blue massive stars. This data volume renders traditional spectral classification techniques increasingly impractical. We aim to develop a robust ML framework for the automated spectral classification of massive OB stars by assessing several tree-based ensemble algorithms. Using a large catalog of high-quality optical spectra of OB stars, we design 3 hierarchical experiments of increasing complexity: classification into broad SpT; fine-grained classification within the O and B domains; and joint classification of SpT and LC. We evaluate 6 algorithms, ranging from single Decision Trees to ensemble methods and gradient boosting techniques. We further analyze model consensus and probabilistic outputs, and employ SHAP value analysis to provide an interpretation of the model decisions by identifying the features that drive each classification. Models achieve excellent performance for broad SpT classification, with LGBM reaching an accuracy of 98%.

Abstract
Behçet’s disease (BD) in childhood is characterised by recurrent inflammatory flares that can result in significant morbidity, most notably with ocular, mucocutaneous, and musculoskeletal manifestations. Timely detection of impending flares is difficult in routine practice, and digital health technologies coupled with patient-reported symptom diaries have been proposed as a candidate route to real-time disease surveillance. As a first methodological step before any prospective evaluation in real patients, we set out to demonstrate that a diary-based machine learning (ML) pipeline can recover a transparent, rule-based flare definition under fully controlled in silico conditions, and to characterise the behaviour of such a pipeline before any clinical deployment is considered. A synthetic, longitudinally structured BD dataset was generated in silico, comprising 100 virtual pediatric patients each followed daily for 90 days (9000 patient-day observations). No real patient data were collected; the dataset was constructed solely as a methodological proof-of-concept and is not presented as a substitute for prospectively collected clinical observations. All simulation parameters were drawn from published pediatric BD distributions and are fully documented in Supplementary Table S1.

parallel-turbo.snippet:
Nested cross-validation (nCV) is a common approach that chooses the classification model and features to represent a given outer fold based on features that give the maximum inner-fold accuracy.

...

nCV is an effective way to incorporate feature selection and machine-learning parameter tuning to train an optimal prediction model. In the standard nCV approach, data is split into k outer folds and then inner folds are created in each outer training set to select features, tune parameters and train models. Using an inner nest limits the leaking of information between outer folds that feature selection can cause, and consequently the inner nest prevents biased outer-fold CV error estimates for independent data.

...

The model and hyperparameters with lowest overfitting across the inner folds is chosen as the training outer-loop model and tested on the outer-loop test fold.

Commonly used approaches to model selection are based on predictive scores and include information criteria such as Akaike's information criterion, and cross validation. Based on data splitting, cross validation is particularly versatile because it can be used even when it is not possible to derive a likelihood (e.g., many forms of machine learning) or count parameters precisely (e.g., mixed-effects models).

...

There are many variants of cross validation, each characterized by different data-splitting schemes. A commonly used scheme is k -fold, where the available data is split into k (approximately) equal-sized subsets (i.e., “folds”)

...

When using cross validation for both model selection and tuning, hyperparameters must be tuned separately for each training set using an additional inner layer of cross validation; this is called nested cross validation (Cawley & Talbot, 2010 ). Although it can be computationally expensive, nested cross validation is necessary to mitigate overfitting and place all models on an equal footing.

## Why Model Comparison Needs Two Layers

A model comparison often involves more than choosing between fitted algorithms. The analyst may also choose a tuning parameter, such as the number of neighbors in a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) model, or a tree-complexity setting. If the same validation results are used both to make those choices and to claim how well the chosen procedure predicts new observations, the reported performance tends to be too favorable. The comparison has adapted to the particular validation folds.

**Nested cross-validation** separates these tasks. The inner folds select a model and its tuning settings using only an outer training set. The outer fold, which was not used for those choices, evaluates the selected procedure. Repeating this process across outer folds estimates the performance of the process that includes model selection—not just the performance of a model chosen in advance.

**Definition:** In nested cross-validation, **inner cross-validation** compares candidate models or settings within each outer training set. The selected candidate is refitted using that full outer training set, then evaluated on its corresponding **outer test fold**. The outer-fold results are combined to estimate predictive performance.

Suppose there are \(n\) observations and the outcome is \(Y\). For classification, one possible loss is the indicator of an incorrect class prediction, \(L(Y,\hat{Y})=I(Y\ne\hat{Y})\). For regression, a common loss is squared error, \(L(Y,\hat{Y})=(Y-\hat{Y})^2\). Cross-validation averages a chosen loss over held-out observations. The metric and loss should be selected for the prediction task; the nested structure does not itself choose them.

## Chapter 9: Decision Trees — Learning by Asking Questions

The linear models we've built so far — linear regression, logistic regression — draw straight lines through data. They're interpretable, efficient, and principled. But the world isn't always linear.

Consider this pattern in the house price data: small houses in premium neighborhoods sometimes cost more than large houses in average neighborhoods. Size and price don't have a simple linear relationship — the relationship depends on the interaction between size *and* neighborhood. A linear model can struggle to capture this.

A decision tree takes a completely different approach. Instead of fitting a line, it asks questions: "Is the square footage above 2,000? If yes, is the neighborhood quality above 7? If yes, predict $420,000. If no, predict $310,000." It partitions the feature space into rectangular regions, assigning a constant prediction to each region.

This is remarkably flexible — and remarkably interpretable.

## 9.1 The Core Idea: Recursive Partitioning

### Definition: Decision Tree

A **decision tree** is a hierarchical model that makes predictions by asking a series of yes/no questions about the input features. Each internal node tests a feature; each branch corresponds to a test outcome; each leaf node contains a prediction.

For regression, the prediction at each leaf is the mean of training examples reaching that leaf. For classification, it's the majority class (or a class probability distribution).

The tree is built by **recursive partitioning**: at each node, choose the feature and split value that best separates the data according to some criterion. Recurse on each resulting subset until a stopping criterion is met.

├── No: Is age < 20 years?
│   ├── Yes: Predict $295,000
│   └── No: Predict $218,000

1. Decision trees

   Describe **recursive binary splitting** used to grow a decision tree, and why it is a greedy top-down algorithm.

   Starting with all observations in one region, the algorithm searches over every predictor $X_j$ and cutpoint $s$ and picks the split into $\{X_j<s\}$ and $\{X_j\ge s\}$ that most improves the objective (lowest RSS for regression, lowest impurity for classification). It then recurses **independently** within each resulting region. It is **top-down** (begins at the root, works toward the leaves) and **greedy** (each split is chosen to be best *at that step*, not looking ahead to splits that might be better later). Greediness makes it fast but not guaranteed to find the globally optimal tree.

2. Decision trees

   For a **regression tree**, what quantity does each split minimize, and what value is predicted in a terminal region?

The prediction in a terminal region (leaf) $R_j$ is the **mean of the training responses** in that region: $\hat y_{R_j}=\frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i\in R_j}y_i$. ## The problem: deciding by asking questions

Ask someone how they decide whether a fruit is ripe and they will not describe a hyperplane. They will describe a chain of questions: is it yellow? if so, is it soft? if not, does it smell sweet? Each question looks at one property, and the answer decides which question comes next. A **decision tree** turns that habit into a model. It is one of the most widely used supervised learners, and also one of the least understood in theory: for the linear methods and SVMs of the earlier modules there are results on convergence, bias and variance, but for trees we can state the problem and the best-known heuristic for it, and only isolated special cases say how close that heuristic gets to the best possible tree.

This module covers trees in the order the lectures do. This lesson starts with regression, where every leaf outputs a number; later lessons stop and prune the tree, move to classification, and deal with categorical and missing values.

## Recursive binary splits and rectangles

Take two inputs \(x_1, x_2\) in the unit square. The first question is "is \(x_1 < 0.6\)?", which cuts the square into a left and a right part. Each part then gets its own question. On the left we might ask "is \(x_2 < 0.5\)?", on the right "is \(x_2 < 0.2\)?". The square is now four rectangles, \(R_1\) to \(R_4\), and the same partition is drawn as a tree: the root holds the first question, each internal node holds a later one, and each **leaf** is one region.

One partition, two drawings. Every cut is parallel to an axis, and each later cut applies only inside the part it was made in: the left half is cut at \(x_2 = 0.5\), the right half at \(x_2 = 0.2\). Going left in the tree means "yes".

Two assumptions hide in this picture. The regions are rectangles with sides parallel to the axes, because every question tests one variable against one number.

## Training vs inference in machine learning.

**Training** — the model learns patterns from data by adjusting weights to minimise a loss function. Computationally expensive; done offline or periodically.

**Inference** — using the trained model to make predictions on new, unseen data. Must be fast and reliable for production serving.

Training uses backward propagation and optimisers (Adam, SGD). Inference is forward-pass only.

## Classification vs regression.

**Classification** — predict a *category* (discrete label). Binary (spam/not spam) or multi-class (cat/dog/bird). Output: class probabilities.

**Regression** — predict a *continuous number*. Example: house price, temperature, revenue forecast. Output: a real-valued number.

Same algorithms can do both with different loss functions and output layers.

## Overfitting vs underfitting.

**Overfitting** — model memorises training data (including noise) and fails on new data. Signs: high training accuracy, low validation accuracy. Fixes: more data, regularisation, simpler model, dropout, early stopping.

   Describe **recursive binary splitting** and why it is a *greedy*, *top-down* algorithm.

   Starting from the full predictor space, the algorithm scans every predictor $X_j$ and every cutpoint $s$ and chooses the single split into half-planes $\{X_j<s\}$ and $\{X_j\ge s\}$ that most improves the objective. It then repeats within each resulting region until a stopping rule fires. **Top-down:** it begins at the root and works downward. **Greedy:** at each step it takes the best split *right now*, never looking ahead to whether a worse split now would enable a better tree later — so the tree is not guaranteed globally optimal.

2. Regression trees

   State the **splitting criterion** for a regression tree and the prediction rule in each leaf.

   A regression tree partitions the space into $M$ boxes $R_1,\dots,R_M$ chosen to minimize the residual sum of squares $\text{RSS}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{i\in R_m}(y_i-\hat y_{R_m})^2$, where $\hat y_{R_m}$ is the **mean response of the training observations in box $R_m$**. We developed scDNM, an adaptation of the dendritic neuron model incorporating learnable synaptic thresholds, a supervised gene pool, staged training, and ensemble prediction. Six binary classification tasks were constructed from the Paul15, PBMC3k, and Nestorowa datasets. All models were evaluated using leakage-free nested cross-validation, with feature selection, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning performed independently of the outer test folds.
